articles.title: South Korea Doubles AI Chip Budget: 4 ETFs to Ride the Wave - TradingView
articles.summary: South Korea Doubles AI Chip Budget: 4 ETFs to Ride the Wave  TradingView
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s president Lee Jae Myung unveiled the country’s largest-ever budget on Monday, raising total spending by 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won (nearly $610.14 billion), with 21.3 trillion won earmarked for semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers — nearly double the 2026 level. A separate 4.7 trillion won will fund a sovereign AI model targeting “world’s highest performance,” alongside training for 2,000 semiconductor design specialists and expanded AI education.
South Korea's increased investment commitment comes amid a surge in semiconductor exports, with October shipments jumping 93.7% year over year to a record $115.3 billion and cumulative exports surpassing $900 billion for the first time.
Considering the fact that South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix dominate the global memory chip supply chain, which is critical for AI accelerators, Seoul’s latest spending push stands to ripple across the entire global AI ecosystem, not just domestically.
For investors, South Korea’s pivotal role in the global AI infrastructure expansion and its record spending commitment could entice them to look for companies positioned to benefit from rising demand for memory, packaging and data center infrastructure. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) offering exposure to these companies could provide a way to capitalize on these growth trends.
Before exploring these ETFs, it is important to examine South Korea’s growing AI momentum and assess how the latest investment commitment could boost the AI industry, with the chip market at the center of attention.
The Chip Rally That Made Seoul a Global AI Hub
South Korea’s semiconductor industry has been the engine behind the KOSPI’s meteoric rise, with the benchmark index surging past 8,000 points in May 2026 as AI-driven demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) reshaped the country’s equity market.
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, two of the world’s three largest memory chipmakers, have been the primary accelerators and beneficiaries.
Samsung’s shares have climbed roughly 190% over a six-month period in May, while SK Hynix gained about 220% as orders for advanced memory used in AI data centers soared.
It is imperative to mention in this context that SK Hynix alone holds approximately 50% of the global HBM market, making it a critical supplier to AI accelerator ecosystems. The rally has been so pronounced that SK Hynix became the second South Korean company to top 1,500 trillion won in market value.
This concentration of memory leadership in a single country is precisely why Seoul’s budget decisions carry outsized weight for global AI infrastructure.
Benefits of the Budget Pledge and the Case for ETFs
The 21.3 trillion won allocation for 2027 spans semiconductors, physical AI, and AI data centers, while 2.1 trillion won goes toward electricity and water infrastructure for chip plants that require uninterrupted power.
The expected outcome from this spending target is not merely higher output but a deepening of South Korea’s moat across the entire value chain: memory, packaging, substrates, testing and equipment.
For investors, picking individual winners in this ecosystem is difficult because the beneficiary list extends well beyond Samsung and SK hynix into materials, components and infrastructure firms.
ETFs solve this by offering diversified, single-ticker access to the Korean AI semiconductor value chain, capturing both the memory leaders and the smaller suppliers that stand to benefit from the government’s spending push.
Beyond Korea-specific funds, ETFs holding semiconductor companies worldwide also stand to gain. Notably, global chip ETFs capture the accelerator demand that South Korea’s increased capex in data center and chip production would generate. For example, NVIDIA NVDA through GPU procurement for sovereign AI and hyperscaler buildouts, AMD via its government-level heterogeneous computing partnership, and Broadcom through custom AI chip and HBM collaboration with Samsung and SK Hynix.
ETFs Positioned for the Upside
Considering the aforementioned discussion, the following ETFs should benefit from South Korea’s latest capex pledge:
iShares MSCI South Korea ETF EWY
This fund, with net assets worth $22.40 billion, offers exposure to 76 companies in South Korea. SK Hynix (holding 23.76% of this fund’s assets), Samsung Electronics (23.02%) and SK Square (2.96%) hold the first three positions in this fund.
EWY charges 59 basis points (bps) in fees. It traded at a good volume of 14.82 million shares in the last trading session.
VanEck Semiconductor ETF SMH
This fund, with net assets worth $64.52 billion, offers exposure to 26 companies involved in semiconductor production and equipment. NVDA (20.19%), Taiwan Semiconductor (9.58%) and Texas Instruments (5.70%) hold the first three positions in this fund. SK Hynix holds the 10th position in this fund, carrying a 4.14% weight.
SMH charges 35 bps in fees. It traded at a good volume of 8.61 million shares in the last trading session.
xETFs Korea AI Semiconductor ETF KSMH
This fund, with net assets worth $1.39 million, includes 10 to 25 Korean companies powering the AI semiconductor value chain, including memory, logic, manufacturing and infrastructure. SK Hynix (22.35%), Samsung Electronics (20.49%) and Hanmi Semiconductor (7.73%) hold the first three positions in this fund.
KSMH charges 65 bps in fees. It traded at a volume of 0.001 million shares in the last trading session.
iShares Semiconductor ETF SOXX
This fund, with net assets worth $42.97 billion, includes 30 companies across the semiconductor value chain, including those driving innovation in AI and benefiting from capital investments in digital infrastructure. Advanced Micro Devices AMD (9.24%), NVDA (7.98%), Micron Technology MU (7.95%) and Broadcom AVGO (7.58%) hold the first four positions in this fund.
SOXX charges 33 bps in fees. It traded at a good volume of 10.78 million shares in the last trading session.

articles.title: North Korea laundering Binance billions with Chinese help — to spend on new missiles - New York Post
articles.summary: North Korea laundering Binance billions with Chinese help — to spend on new missiles  New York Post
articles.full_text:
For that they have Chinese brokers and middlemen who turn the loot into useable funds, which Kim Jong Un’s regime will undoubtedly spend on weapons and missiles, experts told The Post.
“There’s not much to buy in Pyongyang. What North Korea needs to advance its missile program and its nuclear weapons development program is stuff that exists outside North Korea.
“Stealing cryptocurrency gives North Korea a sort of international slush fund that it can move around the world without using banks, and it can pay people off, and buy the stuff that it needs,” Geoff White, author of “The Lazarus Heist” which investigates North Korea’s hackers told The Post.
Chinese laundering crews are believed to have taken over after the hackers’ initial transfers within 20 minutes of the hack last week, according to Nick Carlsen, an investigator at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs.
The speed of the theft was astonishing. Most of the Binance funds moved across 10 blockchains in about 20 minutes, according to TRM. Attackers then raced to swap assets issuers were able to freeze for unsanctioned cryptocurrencies beyond their control.
“From that point on, it’s almost exclusively Chinese money laundering teams that are actually doing all of the transactions,” he told The Post.
In its first three and a half days, the laundering operation then used about 12,000 digital wallets—roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds—according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic. The transfers complicated tracking but have not make the money untraceable.
Carlsen said the stolen money adds to the regime’s coffers, helping fund its spending priorities.
“These massive inflows of hard currency go to the regime, allowing it to pursue its priorities,” he told The Post. “Lately the highest priorities are weapons development and internal improvements.”
The security experts pointed out North Korea’s hackers may not necessarily be stationed in the country, which helps operators blend into other countries’ internet traffic.
“We know that North Korean hackers have pitched up in China and been working from there,” White said.
Carlsen said TRM had observed overlap between the Binance laundering and a Chinese network handling earlier North Korean thefts. The money men work for a percentage, eventually exchanging crypto for yuan in Chinese bank accounts or access to payment cards.
“There’s this entire parallel banking system that allows the Chinese to access hard currency overseas, and that’s the networks the North Koreans hide their activity in,” he said.
White pointed out China’s restrictions on making overseas transfers has helped create demand for underground services. From China, the laundered money will likely be moved again.
White pointed to Ramon Abbas, the Nigerian Instagram influencer known as Hushpuppi, known for flaunting luxury clothing and his enviable life in Dubai.
“By night, he was working with all sorts of criminal elements including with North Korean hackers, to move money around to launder money and to facilitate fraud,” White said.
US prosecutors said Abbas supplied Romanian and Bulgarian bank-account details in a conspiracy to launder money from a Maltese bank heist attributed to North Korean hackers. Arrested in Dubai in June 2020, he was sentenced to 135 months in US prison in November 2022.
Carlsen sees more opportunity in targeting the money men than catching hackers protected by their home state.
“From several past recent hacks we’ve identified Hong Kong and China-based individuals that are handling the laundering,” he said.
A 2023 prosecution accused North Korean banker Sim Hyon Sop of working with Chinese and Hong Kong traders to convert stolen crypto into dollar payments for goods for the regime, using Hong Kong front companies.
A separate indictment alleged Sim and Chinese intermediaries procured a Russian helicopter for North Korean customers in 2019. The contract listed a $300,000 price and delivery to a North Korean port.
Carlsen said getting the funds back would only be possible with Chinese co-operation.
“If the Chinese government crack down on illicit banking, period, this would be basically impossible for the North Koreans,” he said. “But if they even just narrowly target the individuals handling these thefts, the North Koreans would be stuck with crypto assets that they can’t sell.”

articles.title: South Korea’s dream of AI autonomy lays bare contradiction within the alliance with the US - Global Times
articles.summary: South Korea’s dream of AI autonomy lays bare contradiction within the alliance with the US  Global Times
articles.full_text:
Photo: VCG
South Korea's ambitious $1 trillion chip bet is facing pressure from its most important ally, the US. According to media reports, President Lee Jae-myung plans to build a major semiconductor cluster in southwestern South Korea. Washington, however, wants more of Seoul's AI expansion to happen in the US. What appears to be a conventional industrial investment project has become a new window into the competing interests within the US-South Korea alliance.
The fundamental divide between the two countries is not whether to develop the semiconductor industry, but who will control advanced manufacturing capabilities and share the industrial dividends of the AI era.
First, the US wants not only semiconductors manufactured by South Korean companies, but also the capacity to manufacture semiconductors on American soil. In the past, the US and South Korea maintained a relatively stable division of labor in the semiconductor industry: The US held advantages in chip design, core technologies and markets, while Samsung and SK Hynix made South Korea a global hub for memory-chip manufacturing. Washington is now increasingly dissatisfied with simply purchasing Korean chips. It wants South Korean companies to transfer more capital, technology and production capacity to the US to support its manufacturing reshoring and supply-chain localization.
South Korea is not unwilling to cooperate. Samsung has already built an advanced foundry in Texas, while SK Hynix is investing in an advanced high-bandwidth memory packaging fab in Indiana. Yet Washington continues to press for greater investment. South Korea, meanwhile, needs to expand domestic production to preserve its semiconductor advantage. If new investment, jobs and advanced manufacturing capabilities increasingly flow to the US, South Korea risks gradually weakening its own industrial base. 
More ironically, while the US urges South Korean companies to build factories there, it has failed to adequately resolve problems involving skilled technical personnel and cross-border labor. In September 2025, US law enforcement authorities detained more than 300 South Korean nationals at the site of a Korean-invested factory project in Georgia, shocking South Korean society and exposing tensions within Washington's manufacturing reshoring agenda.
Second, South Korea is unwilling to remain merely a chip supplier to the US' AI industry. Although Samsung and SK Hynix enjoy significant advantages in advanced memory chips, South Korea still has weaknesses in foundational AI models, computing platforms and software ecosystems. The Lee administration hopes to capitalize on the AI boom by building on its semiconductor manufacturing strengths to develop data centers, computing infrastructure and AI applications, transforming South Korea from a semiconductor powerhouse into an AI powerhouse. South Korea wants to retain more of the technological, financial and employment benefits of AI development at home, rather than relying solely on chip exports to the US. This ambition inevitably conflicts with Washington's push for greater Korean investment in the US.
South Korea's pursuit of industrial autonomy is increasingly colliding with its dependence on the US for security.
The Gwangju project is a case in point. South Korea plans to relocate an existing military airfield and build a major semiconductor cluster on the vacated land. However, the airfield is associated with joint US-South Korean military operations, so its relocation requires coordination with the US. South Korean media have reported that the US military is still carrying out construction projects at the Gwangju airfield. This means that even when South Korea has established a major industrial development plan, it cannot fully determine the timetable for its implementation independently. There is currently insufficient evidence to conclude that Washington is deliberately using the airfield relocation to obstruct South Korea's semiconductor development. Nevertheless, the case illustrates how US-South Korean military arrangements can become an important variable in South Korea's industrial policy.
These show that the US-South Korea alliance is not free of contradictions: Their security cooperation coexists with persistent conflicts of interest. Washington wants Seoul to assume greater security responsibilities, invest more in the US economically, and align its technology and supply chains with American priorities. South Korea, meanwhile, seeks American security guarantees while strengthening its own defense capabilities and preserving room for its domestic strategic industries. The two countries share some objectives, but their interests are not entirely aligned.
South Korea does retain some room for maneuver. The US' AI industry remains highly dependent on advanced memory chips from Samsung and SK Hynix, whose technologies and manufacturing capabilities cannot be fully replaced in the short term. Their semiconductor relationship, therefore, remains deeply complementary, and the two countries are more likely to keep adjusting the distribution of benefits through a combination of cooperation and competition than to enter outright confrontation.
South Korea's fundamental dilemma, however, remains unresolved. Greater investment in the US may ease some economic and trade pressures, but it does not necessarily secure greater strategic autonomy. Its semiconductor strengths may enable it to benefit from the AI boom, but South Korea may still be unable to determine independently where its most advanced production capacity is located. This is the deeper contradiction beneath the surface of the US-South Korea alliance.
The author is the director and professor of the Center for Korean Peninsula Studies at the Shanghai University of International Business and Economics. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

articles.title: South Korea targets sovereign AI amid $15.8bn data centre push - National Technology News
articles.summary: South Korea targets sovereign AI amid $15.8bn data centre push  National Technology News
articles.full_text:
The South Korean government has announced an ambition to develop a world-leading sovereign AI model, part of a major AI investment package intended to accelerate the country’s domestic AI sector.
Lee Jae Myung, the president of South Korea, confirmed in his 2 November budget speech that his government will spend 4.7 trillion won ($3.49 billion) to develop a sovereign AI model with the “world’s highest performance”. 
Sovereign AI has emerged as a growing area of focus for governments working to provide AI functionality for critical national infrastructure and defence without reliance on companies based outside their borders.
Notable sovereign AI models include the French developer Mistral’s Large 4 and German model maker Aleph Alpha’s Kolibri. The UK government has committed at least £560 million to its Sovereign AI Fund, including a further £60 million announced ahead of last week’s budget.
Alongside the sovereign AI commitment, Lee committed to spending $15.86 billion on AI in 2027, including domestic AI development and the rapid buildout of chip manufacturing plants and AI data centres. 
“We will invest 21.3 trillion won, nearly twice this year's amount, in AI and the three megaprojects of semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centres,” Lee said.
Lee previously announced the spending in August, with the aim of doubling down on the growing success of the South Korean AI sector.
This is currently dominated by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, respectively the world’s fourth and sixth largest semiconductor manufacturers, which have become critical suppliers of the hardware necessary for AI data centres and are generating increasingly large receipts for the South Korean government.
In October, Samsung Electronics reported a third quarter operating profit of 107.4 trillion won ($79.98 billion), a 787 per cent year on year increase. SK Hynix reported an operating profit of 83.3 trillion won ($62.04 billion) over the same period.

articles.title: [Column] The South Korea-US security meeting can wait - 한겨레
articles.summary: [Column] The South Korea-US security meeting can wait  한겨레
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump adjusts his cap as he speaks during a midterm campaign rally at Salina Regional Airport in Salina, Kansas, US, Nov. 1, 2026. (Reuters/Yonahp)
          
            
          By Jung E-gil, senior international affairs writer
The US midterm elections on Tuesday mark a major turning point for Seoul’s relations with Washington and its foreign policy more broadly. The outcome will have a profound impact on the domestic and foreign policies of US President Donald Trump, who has plunged both his own country and the international community into turmoil.
Even if the Democrats win, Trump could refuse to accept the results or simply ignore them and double down on his policies. His threat to resume attacks on Iran after the midterms is a case in point. Nevertheless, an election defeat would undermine Trump’s authority and his ability to carry out his agenda.
Trump’s signature initiatives — including his war against Iran, his efforts to end the war in Ukraine, and his trade and tariff campaign against countries around the world — have ground to a halt over the past few months. Facing resistance from the countries affected, Trump has put off further negotiations until after the midterms.
Despite Trump’s threats to resume attacks, Iran has steadfastly refused to negotiate unless the seven conditions in its seven-day confidence-building plan are met. Those conditions include the US lifting its naval blockade and releasing frozen assets.
Separately, Russia has agreed to participate in US-mediated three-party talks with Ukraine but postponed them until after the midterms. Moscow has secured partial relief from US sanctions, including restrictions on diesel exports, while refusing to budge on its current conditions for ending the fighting.
Canada, which has been one of the fiercest opponents of Trump’s trade onslaught, also persuaded him to withdraw the 50% tariffs he had imposed before postponing a new trade agreement until the midterms are over.
While discussing the two countries’ trade talks on Oct. 26, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that “to the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the US is coming closer to our position.”
“Carney described a ‘slight, slight intensification’ of discussions but said Canada’s negotiating position remained unchanged,” the Associated Press reported.
These countries are resisting Trump and applying pressure to extract some concessions for now on the assumption that his self-defeating domestic and foreign policies will lose momentum after the midterms.
In Korea, President Lee Jae Myung has also neatly deflected the Trump administration’s aggressive demands ahead of the election.
At a press conference in September, President Lee drew a bright line on deploying troops to the Strait of Hormuz, declaring that Korea would not deploy troops “for involvement or intervention in a war.”
There are concerns that the measures Lee did mention, including adjustments to the naval Cheonghae Unit’s operational area, could amount to an indirect deployment. But even those questions can be deferred for negotiations after the war with Iran ends. Lee’s announcement deflated not only US demands for a Korean deployment to Hormuz but also domestic calls for Korea to comply.
Seoul also rebutted Trump’s unilateral announcement that Korea would invest US$50 billion in building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska, making clear that no formal agreement had been reached.
Trump piled on pressure, saying, “If they don’t want to do it, that’s OK with me. I’ll just charge them more.” Trump repeated the warning: “Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m going to double it up.”
But even the US Commerce Department had to sheepishly acknowledge that no such agreement exists with Korea.
US foreign policy has become a snarl of contradictions. While pledging to stay out of overseas conflicts, Trump has kicked off a war against Iran — which keeps the US from concentrating its forces or rallying its allies in East Asia, which ought to be its principal strategic theater.
This helps explain why Gen. Xavier Brunson, the commander of US Forces Korea, has described the Korean Peninsula as a geopolitical “dagger” aimed at China and publicly challenged the transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON), an issue that ought to be decided by the two countries. The fact that a regional military commander is taking on such an outsize role illustrates Washington’s anxiety over, and confusion about, East Asia.
The annual Korea-US Security Consultative Meeting, originally scheduled for the end of this year, has been postponed until next year.
Some in Korea have made a great fuss about the postponement, portraying it as evidence of friction in a fraying alliance. But do they really think that Seoul should accommodate every one of Trump’s unreasonable demands?
If Seoul and Washington disagree over postponing the OPCON transfer or over the US’ strategic goal of turning the Korean Peninsula into a base against China, they should postpone the meeting and work out their differences. For Korea, such a delay might be a blessing in disguise.
After the midterms, the Trump administration will have to grapple with an array of countries over its pending foreign policy disputes, not to mention crossing swords with the Democrats at home.
Carney has previously warned that Washington’s signature was sometimes “written in pencil.” Asked on Oct. 26 whether Trump would “sign in pen” on a new trade agreement, the Canadian premier replied, “I don’t know that,” making clear he intends to combat Trump’s penchant for reneging on deals he has made.
That is precisely why Korea must also draw a clear line about Trump’s unreasonable demands, particularly after the midterms.
A crisis can turn out to be an opportunity.
If the US is thrown into unprecedented turmoil at home and abroad after the elections, it could give Korea a chance to recalibrate its relationship with Washington to better serve its national interest and suit its global status.

articles.title: China Claims Credit as Korea Nears $1 Trillion in Annual Exports - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: China Claims Credit as Korea Nears $1 Trillion in Annual Exports  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
South Korea is on course to become the fourth country to post $1 trillion in annual exports, and China's state media is highlighting what it says is the contribution of the Chinese market. An artificial intelligence boom has lifted Korean chip exports, the argument goes, but China is one of the key markets generating that demand.
Korean Exports Top $930 Billion, Chip Shipments Surge 259%
Cumulative exports for the January-October period reached $930 billion, passing $900 billion for the first time, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy on the 2nd. That leaves $70 billion to reach $1 trillion for the year. At the current pace, Korea is expected to cross that mark this month, becoming the fourth country to do so after the United States, China and Germany.
Exports in October totaled $115.28 billion, up 93.7% from a year earlier. It was the second-largest monthly export figure on record.
The explosive growth of the AI industry drove the increase. October semiconductor exports came to $56.44 billion, up 259.4% year-on-year, as global big tech companies expanded investment in AI data centers and sharply increased chip demand.
Computer exports jumped 496.6% to $5.85 billion, reflecting stronger demand for solid-state drives used in AI servers. Exports of electrical equipment needed for AI infrastructure, including transformers and power cables, rose 74%.
The strength was not confined to any single region. Exports to China rose 133.6% to $26.98 billion, while shipments to the United States climbed 185.8% to $24.9 billion. Exports to Southeast Asian nations increased 128% to $21.33 billion.
Chinese Media Says Demand From China's AI Sector Played a Part
Global Times, a Chinese state-run English-language outlet, addressed Korea's prospects of reaching $1 trillion in exports in a commentary on the 2nd and stressed the importance of the Chinese market.
The outlet said Korea's export surge is tied to expanding AI investment worldwide. It framed the AI industry not as a sector limited to chips or software but as a vast supply chain linking data centers, power equipment and other industries.
China's role in that supply chain is growing, the outlet argued. Citing the 133.6% rise in Korea's October exports to China, Global Times said China's expanding technology industry is generating demand that crosses borders.
It also pushed back against assessments in some quarters that Chinese demand is weakening, saying China is increasing technology exports while also expanding imports of foreign products, creating business opportunities for companies in other countries.
Such two-way trade makes China an important participant in the expansion of global trade in the AI era, the outlet said.
The commentary acknowledged Korea's export performance while emphasizing that ties to the Chinese market contributed to that growth.
Supply Chain Cooperation Called Key to Sustaining $1 Trillion
Global Times said Korea needs to strengthen cooperation with international supply chains not only to reach $1 trillion in exports but also to maintain growth beyond that point.
Citing the World Trade Organization's 2025 World Trade Report, the outlet said AI could expand cross-border trade in goods and services by about 40% by 2040 through productivity gains and lower trade costs, if backed by appropriate policies.
Deeper integration with global supply chains and trade openness are important if Korea is to sustain export growth, the outlet said.
Industrial cooperation and an open trading environment are the key conditions for further export expansion, it argued. The message can also be read as saying that Korea and other exporting countries need to maintain their links to global production and trade networks, including China.
The Korean government, for its part, plans to strengthen trade cooperation with major economies to keep export growth going.
"Reaching $1 trillion in annual exports during November is now all but certain," Trade Minister Kim Jung-kwan said on the 1st. "We will concentrate all of our policy capacity so that small and mid-sized companies can also broadly share in the gains from export growth."

articles.title: US Midterm Forecast: The Key Risks for Traders to Watch Through the US Elections - StoneX
articles.summary: US Midterm Forecast: The Key Risks for Traders to Watch Through the US Elections  StoneX
articles.full_text:
Prediction markets are pricing in nearly 75% odds of a Democratic sweep in this week’s US midterm elections, a development that would result in a split from the single party Republican rule of the past two years - what will it mean for markets?
US MIDTERM KEY TAKEAWAYS:
- Prediction markets are pricing in nearly 75% odds of a Democratic sweep in this week’s US midterm elections, a development that would result in a split from the single party Republican rule of the past two years.
- Markets are always forward-looking, and a divided government is now the base case, so volatility may be relatively subdued if the results ultimately follow the script.
- A too-close-to-call result or delayed count could be one of the biggest risks, keeping short-term volatility elevated and likely weighing on the US dollar and US indices until there is confidence in the outcome.
US voters head to the polls on Tuesday, November 3, to elect all 435 members of the House and 35 senators. Prediction markets are pricing in nearly 75% odds of a Democratic sweep, a development that would result in a split from the single party Republican rule of the past two years.
Source: Kalshi
Crucially, it’s worth noting that markets are always forward-looking, and a divided government is now the base case, so volatility may be relatively subdued if the results ultimately follow the script.
For markets, the ultimate result may matter less than whether it surprises. If Democrats take both chambers, a Republican president would face a Congress less likely to support new fiscal stimulus or major legislation. But the administration would retain significant influence over tariffs and other policy areas through executive actions. A change in congressional control could still mean more hearings and scrutiny, especially around technology, crypto and the rapid expansion of data centers.
For traders, the status of the vaunted “AI Trade” is one of the most important considerations. Rising public concern about data centers, electricity costs and their impact on local communities could bring more regulatory attention or delay projects. That could unsettle companies tied to AI infrastructure, even if it does not derail the longer-term investment cycle.
The dollar’s reaction will likely depend on Treasury yields, rate expectations and risk sentiment more than the result alone. A Republican sweep could revive expectations for further fiscal expansion, potentially supporting yields and the dollar. A Democratic sweep could constrain new fiscal initiatives, but existing tariff policy may not change quickly. If the expected outcome arrives, traders may see little lasting movement as attention returns to the Federal Reserve, economic data and corporate earnings.
Election results will come in Tuesday evening and night, but the new Congress does not take office until January 3. That gap limits the prospect of an immediate policy shift. Indeed, a too-close-to-call result or delayed count could be one of the biggest risks, keeping short-term volatility elevated and likely weighing on the US dollar and US indices until there is confidence in the outcome. still stir short-term volatility, though the election is only one of several competing forces this week.
US Dollar Technical Analysis – DXY Daily Chart
Source: TradingView, StoneX
For forex traders, the 101.50 area on the US Dollar Index is a key technical level. The index is testing that zone after it previously acted as resistance and then support. A clear break lower could put the 100.50 area in view; holding above it would keep the recent range intact. In either case, price action and yields may offer a clearer signal than political headlines alone.
-- Written by Matt Weller, Global Head of Research

articles.full_text:
A struggling Japanese Yen (JPY) helps GBP/JPY move modestly higher on Monday, with hawkish signals from the Bank of Japan (BoJ) failing to lift the currency. The British Pound (GBP), meanwhile, benefits from easing fiscal uncertainty after the UK’s Autumn Budget, with traders now focusing on this week’s Bank of England (BoE) monetary policy announcement. Having briefly moved above 212, the cross is trading near 211.87 at the time of writing, a gain of 0.44% for the day.
Markets have fully factored in a 25-basis-point (bps) rate increase ahead of the BoE’s decision on Thursday, as surging energy costs add to inflation. Policymakers also have scope to increase borrowing costs thanks to stable labour market conditions and growth that has held up.
In ING analysts’ assessment, Sterling is “trading reasonably well,” with support coming from the market’s belief that “high energy prices leave the Bank of England no alternative but to hike rates on Thursday.” In their view, “a 25bp rate hike to 4.00% looks like a done deal,” while the Pound’s sentiment backdrop also benefits from “upside economic surprises, UK fiscal policy seemingly heading in the right direction and warmer ties with the EU,” factors that provide further support for Sterling.
Pointing to the currency’s outlook, OCBC argues that "GBP resilience should extend into early 2027 as fiscal discipline, resilient growth and political stability remain supportive." The bank nevertheless cautions that "with substantial BoE tightening already priced in, further gains will require increasingly positive UK surprises."
For the Japanese Yen (JPY), the BoJ’s hawkish position has not prevented continued pressure. High energy prices are encouraging other central banks to tighten policy as well. With interest rates outside Japan still considerably higher, yield differentials remain wide.
Friday’s widely anticipated BoJ decision left interest rates at 1.25%, although the bank indicated that further increases would follow if economic activity and prices develop in accordance with its forecasts. The full quarterly outlook report, published on Monday, said underlying inflation had climbed towards 2% and was gradually becoming anchored at that level. Further rate rises would likely help moderate price pressures and underpin consumption, the BoJ added.
Fresh intervention warnings have also done little to support the Yen. On Monday, Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama again said the authorities stood ready to respond to disorderly currency movements, adding that Japan’s joint foreign exchange statement with the US was still in effect.

articles.title: Korean retail investors dump Samsung, SK hynix as big tech cash flows strain - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Korean retail investors dump Samsung, SK hynix as big tech cash flows strain  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
Recently, individual investors have been dumping Samsung Electronics(005930) and SK hynix(000660) shares. As concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence (AI) investment flared and the market plunged through mid-Oct., Les Fourmis propped up the index by buying large-cap semiconductor stocks.
But sentiment shifted as earnings from global big tech showed deteriorating cash flow. As more individual investors judged that their AI investment may be hard to sustain, investor sentiment toward the semiconductor sector also appeared to weaken.
On Nov. 2, according to the Korea Exchange (KRX) information data system, individuals net sold 1.7411 trillion won of SK hynix and 1.2270 trillion won of Samsung Electronics in the main market over the past two weeks (Oct. 19–30). They ranked first and second, respectively, by individual net selling amount.
Just two weeks earlier, individuals were trading in the opposite direction. From Oct. 1–18, when caution over AI investment grew as the five-year credit default swap (CDS) premium of AI infrastructure company CoreWeave surpassed 1,100 bps, foreigners net sold nearly 14 trillion won of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix combined, but individuals net bought 4.2991 trillion won of Samsung Electronics and 1.8093 trillion won of SK hynix. The two stocks ranked first and second at the time by individual net buying amount.
The shift in individual judgment toward the semiconductor sector is seen as stemming from the rise in concerns about the sustainability of AI investment.
In particular, during the so-called "super week," when big tech corporations released earnings, it became clear that large-scale AI investment is weighing on cash flow. Meta swung to negative free cash flow (FCF) due to expanded capital expenditures (CAPEX), and Tesla lowered its annual investment plan. Alphabet reported revenue that fell short of market expectations, and with the burden of AI investment expense highlighted, the stock plunged more than 12%.
Over the weekend, news further stoked concerns about AI investment. On Oct. 30 (local time), Amazon's next-12-month forward FCF came in at minus (-) $42.4 billion. Intel also released results that fell short of market expectations. A warning from Blackstone that Anthropic may find it difficult to secure an investment-grade credit rating after its initial public offering (IPO) also added pressure.
Still, brokerages say it is premature to doubt the AI industry's growth solely on big tech's worsening cash flow. Seo Jeong-hoon, a Samsung Securities researcher, said, "The expense burden from AI investment has grown, but the demand and funding capacity to support it remain solid," adding, "Current market concerns surrounding AI-related stocks are somewhat exaggerated."
In fact, big tech's AI revenue growth is steep. Alphabet's cloud segment revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, and Amazon Web Services (AWS) posted growth approaching 40%. Intel's AI-related revenue also rose 78% year over year.
Their funding capacity is also seen as solid. Alphabet succeeded in a $85 billion stock issuance in June, and Microsoft issued $25 billion in corporate bonds at rates below the investment-grade average. The explanation is that, because they can raise funds in the market to continue AI investment, it is hard to deny investment sustainability based solely on deteriorating cash flow.
In addition, the semiconductor cycle remains firm, and the valuation appeal has grown as share prices fell. On the 1st, Oct. exports were reported at $115.3 billion, up 93.7% from a year earlier. Of that, semiconductor exports jumped to $56.4 billion, up 259.4%. The KOSPI 12-month forward price-earnings ratio (PER) also fell to around 4.1 times, entering a historically undervalued range.

The Asia-Pacific currency faces selling pressure despite multiple tailwinds, including a sharp correction in oil prices, Bank of Japan (BoJ) reiterating hawkish monetary policy stance in the policy announcement on Friday, and Tokyo warning joint intervention with the United States (US).
As of writing, the WTI Oil price is 2.6% lower to near $99.50. A decline in oil prices bodes well for currencies from economies, such as Japan, given their significant reliance on energy imports.
On Friday, BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda signaled that the central bank will remain on the monetary tightening path after leaving interest rates steady at 1.25%. “BoJ will continue to raise policy rate and adjust degree of monetary easing in response to economic activity, prices and financial condition developments,” Ueda said in the press conference.
Earlier in the day, Japanese Finance Minister (FM) Satsuki Katayama said that the Joint FX statement with the US persists and the government will act against disorderly moves.
Meanwhile, the US Dollar trades lower as investors turn cautious ahead of US midterm elections on Tuesday.
In the daily chart, USD/JPY trades at 157.77. The pair refletcs a braoder sideways trend as the 9-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) at around 157.72 has been flat-lined for over a month.
The Relative Strength Index (RSI) at 50.81 sits near the neutral line, suggesting a balanced momentum amid a sideways trend.
On the downside, the major support is the October low at 156.08. Looking up, the September 24 high at 159.04 is the major hurdle for the pair.

Likewise, if the BoJ has a dovish view on the Japanese economy and keeps interest rates unchanged, or cuts them, it is usually bearish for JPY.
